quote: First, concerning the "lamp" and the "lampstand" and the "oil" which is poured into it; second, concerning the "table" and the "shewbread" and their number and those who ought to use them. Let us therefore direct our mind more diligently to the things that are written, and let us pray that the grace of the Lord be granted us for discerning these things, so that in the letters which we read we may recognize what is the will of the Holy Spirit. "Command", it says, "the children of Israel, and let them bring you clean oil pressed from olives for the light, that a lamp may burn always outside the veil in the tabernacle of testimony, and Aaron and his sons shall kindle it from evening until morning before the Lord without ceasing, an everlasting statute throughout your generations. On the clean lampstand you shall kindle the lamps before the Lord until morning". He names a "clean lampstand";…

But "since the law is spiritual", let us ask of the Lord — if indeed "we have turned to the Lord" — that "the veil of the reading of the old testament be taken away" from us, so that we may be able to perceive what is the meaning of his "lampstand and lamps" according to the spiritual understanding. Before the coming of my Lord Jesus Christ the sun did not rise upon the people of Israel, but it made use of "the light of a lamp". For among them the word of the law and the prophetic word was a "lamp" shut within narrow walls, which could not pour out its light upon the whole earth. For within Judea the knowledge of God was confined, as the prophet also says: "God is known in Judea". But when the "sun of righteousness", our Lord and Savior, rose, and the man was born of whom it is written: "behold a man, the East is his name", throughout the whole world the light of the knowledge of God…

The twelve loaves on the table of the tabernacle then are the twelve apostles and all those in the church who follow their teaching. Since until the end of time they do not cease to renew the people of God with the nourishment of the word, they are the twelve loaves of proposition which never depart from the table of the Lord. And those same loaves are properly ordered to be made not from just any flour but from the finest wheat, doubtless because all those who minister the word of life to others must first devote themselves to the fruits of virtue. [Thus] they may commend by their actions those things that they counsel in their preaching, being conformed to the example of him who says concerning himself, "Unless a grain of wheat falls into the ground and dies, it remains alone." Those same loaves are also properly commanded to be set on the table in two rows of six for the sake of…

In the first place, the figure of the twelve apostles is clearly foretold here in the very number of the loaves, for when the Lord appeared in flesh he chose them to be the first of those by whose ministry he gave the food of life to all nations. And then to these same disciples of his (that is, to our apostles), he says in reference to the multitudes hungering in the wilderness, "You give them something to eat." And when five thousand men had been satisfied from the five loaves, they "gathered twelve baskets of fragments," doubtless because those sacraments of the Scriptures which the multitudes are not able to receive belong to the apostles and the apostolic men.

The Old Covenant had its loaves of proposition, but they, as belonging to that covenant, have come to an end. The New Covenant has its heavenly bread and cup of salvation to sanctify both body and soul. For as the bread is for the body, the Word suits the soul.

But now let us see what is written also in what follows concerning the shewbread. "And you shall take", it says, "fine flour and make from it twelve loaves; of two tenths shall be one loaf; and you shall set them in two rows, six loaves in one row, upon the clean table before the Lord. And you shall put upon the row clean frankincense and salt, and the loaves shall be set as a memorial before the Lord; on the day of the sabbaths they shall always be set forth before the Lord by the children of Israel, an everlasting covenant. And it shall be Aaron's and his sons', and they shall eat them in a holy place; for they are the holy of holies. This shall be theirs of the things that are offered to the Lord, an everlasting statute". According to what is written, in the twelve loaves a "memorial before the Lord" seems to be made of the twelve tribes of Israel, and a command to be given that…

But let us now see what is the making of these shewbread loaves which are commanded to be "always placed before the Lord". "Of two tenths", it says, "let there be one loaf". He said "two tenths" indeed, but of what measure these "tenths" are he did not specify; although surely it would have been consistent, if he wished the quantity of the fine flour to be known, to name the measure itself of which he commanded "two tenths" to be taken. What, then, is this thing whose measure and amount could neither be specified nor named? The number ten is everywhere found to be perfect; for from it arises the reckoning and origin of every number. Fittingly, therefore, the author and origin of all things, God, is seen to be shown under this number. But if in the church I speak of the Father alone and utter the praises of him alone, I have made a loaf of one tenth. Or if I make a discourse concerning…

But let us see how these "twelve loaves" are set forth: "two rows", it says, "six loaves in one row". Do you suppose this division is idle? Why is it that the number twelve is again divided into six? For the number six has a certain kinship with this world; for in six days this visible world was made. Two orders, therefore, are held in this world, that is, two peoples, who guard the faith of the Father and the Son in one church as it were upon "one clean table".

Now that clearest frankincense which is put upon the loaves designates the power of prayer, because the same teachers commit both their ministry of preaching and their labor of devotion unto the Lord. Prayer is symbolized by frankincense, as the psalmist testifies when he says, "Let my prayer be set forth in your sight as incense." The clearest frankincense is put upon the loaves as a memorial of the oblation of the Lord when the pure prayer of the saints is added to their pious action and teaching, so that when each is duly joined to the other, the remembrance of the sacred oblation will always appear in the sight of the supreme Judge.

"And there shall be placed", it says, "upon the row clean frankincense". The kind of frankincense holds the form of prayers. It is fitting, therefore, to join to the loaves of faith the vigilance and purity of prayers. And prayer is pure, as the Apostle says: "lifting up pure hands without wrath and dispute". At the same time the sweetness of the odor also causes to be fulfilled that which is written: "let my prayer be directed as incense in your sight". If anyone, therefore, offers prayers indeed to God, but does not have a conscience clean from evil works, this man seems indeed to "place frankincense" upon the loaves, but not entirely "clean" frankincense. For if all frankincense were "clean", Scripture would surely not have added that "clean frankincense" be "placed before the Lord" upon the shewbread. For do not suppose that almighty God commanded this and sanctioned it by law, that…

The loaves are properly commanded to be changed before the Lord every sabbath day. For surely the loaves that were set out on the table of the Lord through the six days of work are exchanged for new loaves on the sabbath when all the teachers in the holy church, once the time of their holy labor is completed, are rewarded in heaven with eternal peace and leave others behind them in the same work, laboring in the word with the hope of the same reward. And in this way it is brought to pass that the table of the Lord is never left destitute of bread, but as soon as one loaf is taken away another is put in its place, as long as the churches never lack ministers of the word who follow one another in succession. In their words and in their deeds, they always manifest the faith of apostolic piety and the purity of apostolic action, continuing as in that most beautiful verse in which it is said…

And that which is added in conclusion, "And they shall be for Aaron and his sons," contains a mystery which can be understood in two ways. For surely Aaron in company with his sons eats the holy loaves that are taken from the table of the tabernacle when our High Priest takes his elect out of this life and leads them into the increase of his body which is in heaven (that is, the whole multitude of his elect). Or perhaps the holy loaves belong to Aaron and his sons when all the leaders and the peoples who are subjected to them in the Lord are nourished unto life eternal by the examples of the fathers who have gone before.

"An everlasting covenant", it says, "it shall be for Aaron and his sons, and they shall eat them in a holy place". "Aaron and his sons" are "a chosen race, a priestly race", to whom this portion of the holy things is given by God — which we all are who believe in Christ. But I do not seek the "holy place" set on earth, but in the heart. For the rational soul is called a "holy place", for which reason also the Apostle says: "do not give place to the devil". My soul, then, is the place — if I act wickedly, of the devil; if well, of God. Finally also "the evil spirit", it says, "when it has gone out from a man, and has gone about arid places, and has not found rest, then it says: I will return to my place, whence I went out". The "holy place", then, is the pure soul. In which place we are commanded to eat the food of the word of God. For it is not fitting that an unholy soul should receive…

"For they are the holy of holies". You see how he did not say holy only, but "holy of holies", as if he said: this food is not the common food of all, nor of anyone unworthy, but it belongs to "the holy". How much more shall we also say this rightly and deservedly concerning the word of God: this discourse is not for all; not just anyone can hear the mystery of this word, but it belongs only to the holy, who are purified in mind, "who are clean of heart", who are "simple in soul", who are blameless in life, who are free in conscience — theirs it is to hear the discourse concerning this, to them can these mysteries be explained. "For to you it is given", he says, "to know the mysteries of the kingdom of God, but to those", that is, who are not worthy, who are not such as to deserve it nor can be capable of the understanding of secret things, "to those it cannot be given": this priestly…

A narrative has been read to us whose account, though it may seem plain, will nevertheless not easily disclose to us its inner sense unless we follow rather diligently its coherence according to the letter. The passage of Scripture, then, on which we must discourse, is this: "And there went out," it says, "the son of the Israelite woman, and this one was the son of an Egyptian among the sons of Israel; and they quarreled in the camp, he who was of the Israelite woman and a man who was an Israelite. And the son of the Israelite woman, naming the name, cursed; and they brought him to Moses; and the name of his mother was Salomith, the daughter of Dabri, of the tribe of Dan. And they put him into prison, that they might judge concerning him according to the command of the Lord. And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Cast out him who cursed, outside the camp, and all who heard shall lay their…

After these things, now the matters which are recounted in what follows are not without a certain question, concerning which, though many have inquired, not many have been able to explain. But if you help me with your prayers, we too will attempt to bring forward into the midst what the Lord shall grant. "A man, a man," it says, "if he shall curse God, shall receive sin; but he who names the name of the Lord, let him die the death." What is this? He who "shall curse God" does not have the penalty of death, but "he who shall name the name of the Lord"? Is it not far more grievous to "curse God" than to "name" Him, although he is said to have named Him in vain? And how is it that he who "curses" only takes on sin, but he who "names" is punished "with death"? These, then, are the things which in this passage are wont to raise a question, which to those ignorant of the sense of the…

Whosoever by reason of his gluttony destroyeth the members of his body is an associate of the murderer, and he is the consort of a destroying thief, and that which is written in the Law, "Everyone who slayeth shall be slain, and whosoever cutteth off a member of his neighbour, one of his members shall be cut off," applieth unto him. Now the glutton destroyeth his own members, and little by little he maketh to perish and consumeth the power of his body and of his members, and whosoever ruineth the fair creation of God, and throweth down the building of his body which the will of the Architect builded aforetime, bringeth together for every reason punishments upon himself, according to the word of righteousness, which was uttered before he had transgressed the command of God, Who had commanded man not to become a servant unto his lusts.
